summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that a noncustodial parent is entitled to enter a plea and contest a neglect adjudication, including one based on predictive neglect, and affirmed the Appellate Court's reversal on that alternate ground.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Connecticut rule on party rights when the agency files a neglect petition and opens a dependency case.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the father was entitled to contest the neglect adjudication regardless of whether he was a custodial parent

key_cases.holding: The court held that parents stated a justiciable claim for declaratory and injunctive relief against the systemic failure to provide timely evidentiary hearings on orders of temporary custody, and that the trial court improperly struck their request for relief.
key_cases.relevance: The court addresses the six-month delay between the temporary custody order and the combined neglect adjudication, the period this node covers.
key_cases.quote: It is precisely because state intervention can cause irrevocable consequences for both children and parents that "fundamentally fair" procedures provided in a timely manner must be afforded the parties.

key_cases.holding: The court held that termination of parental rights on the acts-of-commission-or-omission ground in § 17a-112 (j)(3)(C) may not rest on predictive harm, but affirmed the judgments because the amended petitions extended the adjudicatory date so that the parents' postremoval conduct, which actually harmed the child, proved the ground.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes what the commissioner must plead and when the adjudicatory date falls once a termination petition is filed and later amended.
key_cases.quote: We agree with the respondents that a termination of parental rights pursuant to § 17a-112 (j) (3) (C) may not be based upon predictive harm.

key_cases.holding: The court held the commissioner was aggrieved by, and could appeal from, the trial court's dismissal of a neglect allegation and that the appeal was not moot.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that a filed neglect petition creates an appealable controversy even after the child's situation changes.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the petitioner is aggrieved by the trial court's dismissal of the neglect allegation and that the appeal is not moot.

key_cases.holding: In a neglect proceeding the court held that a child may be found unavailable, allowing admission of the child's out-of-court statements under the residual hearsay exception, upon case-specific evidence that testifying would cause the child psychological harm.
key_cases.relevance: It controls the proof the commissioner may present at a neglect adjudication after filing the petition.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that a trial court properly may conclude that a child is unavailable if there is competent evidence that the child will suffer psychological harm from testifying

investigation_requirements: Any visit to or evaluation of a home conducted pursuant to a safety plan must be conducted in person, unless a resident of the home is subject to an order of quarantine or isolation (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 17a-101t, P.A. 24-92, effective July 1, 2024)

notice_requirements.timing: At the commencement of any proceeding on behalf of a neglected, uncared-for or abused child or youth, and again at the preliminary hearing on an order of temporary custody or order to appear
content_required: The parent or guardian has the right to counsel and must be so informed by the judge
If the parent or guardian is unable to afford counsel, counsel will be provided
The parent or guardian has the rights of confrontation and cross-examination

The court may also appoint counsel for the parent or guardian without a request if it determines the interests of justice so require (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-136(a)); in a proceeding in which the custody of a child is at issue the judge must provide an attorney for the child

Cost of appointed counsel in the civil juvenile session is shared as agreed by the Division of Public Defender Services and the Judicial Department, and the court may order a party found able to pay to reimburse that cost (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-136(b)(1))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 46b-135 or 46b-136

statutory_basis.citation_text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-135(b) (right to counsel and cross-examination); see also § 46b-136 (appointment of attorney; payment) and § 46b-129(c)(1) (advisement at the preliminary hearing)
